**Psychopathology and treatment** — what a mental disorder is and how psychological treatment changes it — medical models of illness (biomedical, biopsychosocial, network), the philosophy of psychiatry, functional and transdiagnostic accounts of psychopathology such as experiential avoidance and psychological flexibility, and psychotherapies and their mechanisms of change (ADR-021).

A history of behaviour therapy and CBT as empirically grounded treatment development, an argument that common factors are not mechanisms of change, and a proposal: the mechanism of all effective therapies is a shift from a stuck, threat-laden meaning ("Theory A") to a collaboratively built and tested alternative ("Theory B"), which the authors call a type of psychological flexibility. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-428](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-428.md)), from the open-access (CC BY 4.0) publisher PDF; worth reading as a senior Beckian's statement of a single mechanism of change for all effective psychological therapy, and for its clear separation of "common factors" from "mechanisms of change". Its thesis is a proposal argued from the history of CBT and clinical examples, not a tested result: people are "stuck" in an exaggerated negative or threatening meaning (Theory A) kept alive by what it makes them do, and any effective therapy works by helping them build and test a less threatening alternative (Theory B). Relating is a generalized operant learned across exemplars, and its frames share mutual entailment, combinatorial entailment and the transformation of function. | [LIT-547](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-547.md) | A Network Theory of Mental Disorders | Borsboom (2017), World Psychiatry 16(1):5–13. Mental disorders are not common causes of their symptoms but states of networks of symptoms that cause one another, through "myriads of biological, psychological and societal mechanisms". Five principles: disorders are complex systems of interacting components, the components are the symptoms of the diagnostic manuals, the network comes from direct causal connections between symptoms, disorders are the tightly connected clusters, and disorders arise through hysteresis, so a strongly connected network can stay "stuck" after its trigger is gone. Mental health, disorder, resilience and vulnerability are redefined as stable states and dispositions of weakly or strongly connected networks. Its evidence is indirect and it says so: the theory is offered as an "organizing framework" and a deliberate simplification, and the strict symptom-component correspondence of principle 2 is its own flagged weak point. |

| [LIT-586](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-586.md) | Précis of Breakdown of Will | Ainslie (2005), Behavioral and Brain Sciences 28(5), the précis of Breakdown of Will (2001). People and other animals discount delayed rewards hyperbolically, so preferences reverse as a smaller, sooner reward comes near, and a person becomes a population of reward-seeking "interests" that must forestall one another. Willpower is the bundling of future choices by treating the present one as a precedent: an intertemporal repeated prisoner's dilemma, not an organ or a top-down ego. The same recursion predicts the will's costs: legalism, circumscribed "lapse districts", motivated blindness to lapses, and rules that favour countable goals over subtle ones. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-443](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-443.md)), as the substitute for the 2001 book ([LIT-583](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-583.md)), which the owner suggested and which the précis follows chapter by chapter. Worth reading as the shortest complete statement of picoeconomics in Ainslie's own words. Hyperbolic discounting makes preference reverse as a smaller, sooner reward draws near, so a person behaves like a population of "interests" that bargain across time. Will is not a faculty above them but a recursive self-prediction: treating each choice as a precedent "bundles" future rewards, an intertemporal repeated prisoner's dilemma in which "credibility is power". The same mechanism predicts the will's side effects: legalism, "lapse districts", motivated misperception and compulsive over-control. |

Chapter 1 read; the rest unread. | Unavailable — chapter 1 read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-457](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-457.md), Skimmed), from the sample chapter Guilford posts; the other nineteen chapters unread. | [LIT-1263](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1263.md) v2 | Interoceptive inference, emotion, and the embodied self | Seth (2013), Trends in Cognitive Sciences 17(11):565–573, an Opinion article. Emotions are "interoceptive inference": felt states are the content of hierarchical top-down predictions of the causes of interoceptive signals, compared with bottom-up prediction errors in the anterior insula. Prediction errors are also cancelled by action, as descending predictions set the reference points of autonomic reflexes, the visceral counterpart of active inference in motor control. The same scheme is applied to the experience of body ownership. The rubber hand illusion is a revision of the multisensory self-model under precision-weighted error. Low interoceptive sensitivity goes with greater susceptibility to it, and a virtual hand pulsing in time with the heartbeat is owned more. No direct test of the model is claimed. | Active — read in full 2026-10-19 ([NOTE-1000](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1000.md)); worth reading as the short statement that put emotion and body ownership under one predictive-coding mechanism: felt emotion is the content of top-down predictions of the causes of interoceptive signals, the anterior insula is the comparator, and the experience of body ownership is what the brain infers to be "most likely to be me" from interoceptive and exteroceptive signals together. It is an opinion article with no new data. Its evidence is indirect and cited, and its one figure is a study by the author's own group, an augmented-reality rubber hand illusion whose virtual hand flashed in or out of time with the heartbeat. | [LIT-1428](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1428.md) | Psychopathy as a Clinical and Empirical Construct | Hare & Neumann (2008), Annual Review of Clinical Psychology 4:217–246. The PCL-R's items form four correlated factors, Interpersonal, Affective, Lifestyle and Antisocial, explained by one superordinate factor; psychopathy is dimensional, and no component, affective or antisocial, is more essential than the others. Cleckley's Clinical Profile, drawn from an unrepresentative sample, should not be the test of the construct. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1094](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1094.md)): in full, from the copy Hare posts on his own site. Worth reading as the authors' own statement of what the construct is, made while defending it against the charge that the PCL-R has "drifted" from Cleckley. The PCL-R's 20 items fall, 18 of them, into four correlated factors: Interpersonal and Affective (together Factor 1) and Lifestyle and Antisocial (together Factor 2). A single superordinate factor explains them, and the authors hold that no component, the affective one included, is more essential than the others. That is the sharpest constraint the record has on borrowing only the affective features of psychopathy for a corporation. Hare receives royalties from the PCL-R. |

The remedy it proposes is regulation and the democratic control of corporations. Unread: filed from the two descriptions only. | Unavailable — registered 2026-10-23 at the owner's request, not read: no lawful full text was reached. | [LIT-1438](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1438.md) | The current status of research on the structure of evaluative space | Norris, Gollan, Berntson & Cacioppo (2010), Biological Psychology 84(3):422–436. A review of the evaluative space model. The affect system has separable positive and negative channels whose joint output is a bipolar predisposition to approach or avoid. They can be activated reciprocally, independently or together. Coactivation, simultaneous or by fast oscillation, is ambivalence, rare and arousing. Asymmetric activation functions give a negativity bias and a positivity offset, and recalibrate with context. Levels of the neuraxis can override one another. Clinical implications for depression and anxiety. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1101](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1101.md)): in full, from the NIH author manuscript in PubMed Central (PMC2894997, NIHMS165251). Worth reading as the evaluative space model's own later summary, written with Berntson and Cacioppo. Positivity and negativity are separable systems, whose combined output is a bipolar predisposition to approach or withdraw. They can be activated reciprocally, independently or together, and coactivation is ambivalence. Ambivalence and neutrality give the same middling output from different underlying states. Negativity has the higher gain and positivity the higher intercept. It stands in for the unread 1994 and 1997 papers ([LIT-1453](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1453.md), [LIT-1456](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1456.md)). |
| [LIT-1449](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1449.md) | Control Theory, Goal Attainment, and Psychopathology | Carver (2018), Psychological Inquiry 29(3):139–144, a commentary on DeYoung and Krueger. Problems arise wherever a feedback loop's input, reference value, comparison or output is extreme or biased. The five factors are read as sensitivities to classes of goals, not as loop parameters. Valence tracks the velocity of goal attainment against a reference value, so approach and avoidance can each yield either sign. Doubt and disengagement sit outside the loop itself. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1102](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1102.md)): in full, from the NIH author manuscript in PubMed Central (PMC6707771, NIHMS1512534). A short commentary on DeYoung and Krueger's cybernetic theory of psychopathology, and the nearest lawful first-hand statement found of Carver and Scheier's control-process account of affect. Valence is read off the velocity of goal attainment against a reference value. An approach system and an avoidance system can each produce either sign. Many goals are in play at once, and their priorities are juggled. It stands in for the unread 1990 paper ([LIT-1441](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1441.md)). |
| [LIT-1461](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1461.md) | Liking, wanting, and the incentive-sensitization theory of addiction | Berridge & Robinson (2016), American Psychologist 71(8):670–679. 'Wanting' (incentive salience, mesolimbic and dopamine-related) and 'liking' (hedonic impact, small opioid and endocannabinoid hotspots) are dissociable. Repeated, especially intermittent high-dose, drug use can sensitize the 'wanting' system, making it hyper-reactive to drug cues and contexts, lastingly and perhaps permanently, while 'liking' need not rise and may fall. Sensitized 'wanting' can oppose cognitive desire, run without report, and grow during abstinence. Its scope is said to extend, on emerging evidence, to behavioural addictions and to the compulsions of dopamine dysregulation syndrome. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1109](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1109.md)): in full, from the NIH author manuscript in PubMed Central (PMC5171207, NIHMS816820). Worth reading as the authors' own short statement, a quarter-century on, of the incentive-sensitization theory of addiction. Drugs, and perhaps unpredictable non-drug rewards, can make mesolimbic 'wanting' systems lastingly hyper-reactive to cues and contexts, and 'liking' need not rise with it. Sensitized 'wanting' can oppose a person's cognitive desire, operate without report, persist for years and grow during abstinence. It is a review of the authors' programme. Filed for the record's question whether potential of a proxy for maintenance is valence, and the form addiction and metric fixation share ([QUESTION-267](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-267.md)), to which it gives a mechanism on the personal side. |
| [LIT-1465](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1465.md) | A taxonomy of technology design features that promote potentially addictive online behaviours | Flayelle, Brevers, King, Maurage, Perales & Billieux (2023), Nature Reviews Psychology 2(3):136–150. Reviews evidence linking design features to loss of control in online gaming, gambling, cybersexual activity, shopping, social networking and streaming. Proposes a taxonomy based on model-free and model-based learning and control. Model-free: reinforcement schedules (random-ratio rewards such as loot boxes and likes) and personalized triggers (push notifications, recommendations). Model-based: overvaluation of outcomes, features that interfere with deliberation (autoplay, countdowns), partial goal fulfilment (infinite scroll, levels, progress bars) and features that strengthen cognitive biases (near-misses, losses disguised as wins). Providers keep whatever raises use or revenue, and informational asymmetry lets them personalize it. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1096](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1096.md)): in full, from the typeset article as deposited in the University of Lausanne's repository (SERVAL/IRIS). Worth reading as a compact, theory-driven catalogue of the design features of games, gambling, pornography, shopping, social-networking and streaming services that may weaken users' control. Features are sorted by whether they work on model-free learning (reinforcement schedules, personalized cues) or on model-based choice (overvaluation, features that interfere with deliberation, partial goal fulfilment, cognitive biases). It also names the selection process on the provider's side: features that raise use, time-on-device or spending are kept, with no psychology needed. The evidence reviewed is mostly cross-sectional, qualitative or indirect, and the authors warn against pathologizing common behaviour. Filed for the record's question whether potential of a proxy is valence ([QUESTION-267](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-267.md)), because it describes how a firm optimizing its own metric can install proxy-keyed potential in its users. |
| [LIT-1477](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1477.md) v2 | A systematic review of human avoidance learning: Cognition, computation, and methods | Mancinelli & Bach (2026; preprint 2025). A systematic review of 116 studies of avoidance learning in healthy humans with primary reinforcers, analysed for the phenomena a theory must explain and their power to tell theories apart. The evidence contradicts two-factor and other associative theories and favours expectancy and inference-based accounts, though residual avoidance after the outcome is visibly removed contradicts a purely inferential one. An available avoidance response protects threat expectancy from extinction, more so the more effective it is. The common paradigms are simpler than real-world avoidance, so tasks with larger computational demands and more action options are needed. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1134](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1134.md)) from the PsyArXiv preprint, not the closed version of record; worth reading as the only systematic map of human avoidance learning, and for the finding, rated robust, that an available avoidance response protects threat expectancy from extinction, the more so the more effective it is. Avoidance is learned without ending the warning signal and transfers by inference, against two-factor theory; but some avoidance survives visible removal of the outcome, against a purely inferential account. Healthy volunteers with shock or noise only; nothing here is about anxiety disorders. |
| [LIT-1479](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1479.md) v2 | Anxiety as a disorder of uncertainty: implications for understanding maladaptive anxiety, anxious avoidance, and exposure therapy | Brown, Price & Dombrovski (2023; preprint 2022). A narrative review and proposal, with no new data or model run. Cognitive-behavioural accounts put exaggerated threat expectancy behind maladaptive anxiety, but the learning literature (seven computational studies, chosen without a systematic search) fits better a disorder of uncertainty learning: altered adjustment of learning rate to noise and volatility, mostly for aversive outcomes. They propose that in aversive settings avoidance of uncertain states keeps their uncertainty high and so perpetuates itself, that anxiety feeds this by misreading noise as change, and that exposure therapy works by reducing the uncertainty. For fear-based disorders, not GAD. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1120](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1120.md)) from the NIH author manuscript in PubMed Central, not the typeset version of record; worth reading as the clearest statement that anxious avoidance can be kept going by uncertainty that avoidance itself leaves unreduced, with no excess of learned threat needed. A narrative review and proposal: seven computational studies, chosen without a systematic search, show altered adjustment of learning rate to uncertainty, mostly for aversive outcomes; the avoidance loop and the account of exposure are argued in words and schematic figures, not modelled or tested. For fear-based disorders; by the authors' statement it does not explain GAD. |
| [LIT-1480](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1480.md) v2 | Skills‐homework completion and phone coaching as predictors of therapeutic change and outcomes in completers of a DBT intensive outpatient programme | Edwards, Kober, Rinne, Griffin, Axelrod & Cooney (2021). Homework completion correlated with larger falls in suicide and substance-use urges, and coaching with a larger fall in self-harm urges; neither with change in how often the behaviours occurred. Patients free of target behaviours in the final month had completed more homework; the coaching difference was not significant. The authors read both as active ingredients of DBT through generalization. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1121](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1121.md)) from the version of record posted on the Yale lab site of the second author; worth reading as the first study to relate DBT skills homework and phone coaching to outcome, and for how little it can show. Correlational, selected for completed cycles and adequate diary data, uncorrected for multiple comparisons, with no measure of skill use; the abstract states more than the results. |
| [LIT-1483](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1483.md) v2 | The influence of anxiety on exploration: A review of computational modeling studies | Chou, Wilson & Smith (2024). A narrative review of computational modelling studies of how anxiety influences exploration, mostly in reward tasks and sub-clinical samples. In reinforcement-learning tasks directed, but not random, exploration may be raised by trait or cognitive anxiety and lowered by state or somatic anxiety; in foraging tasks anxiety is consistently associated with less exploration, including, in one study, less checking for a predator. Some differences may come from how anxiety modulates learning rates. Results are inconsistent and unreplicated, and tasks, anxiety measures and methods need to be made consistent. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1127](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1127.md)) from the CC BY PsyArXiv preprint, not the closed version of record, whose abstract differs; worth reading as the map of how anxiety relates to exploration once both are split into kinds. In reward bandits directed exploration tends to rise with trait or cognitive anxiety and fall with state or somatic anxiety, random exploration shows no link, and in foraging, and in one task with a predator to check for, anxiety goes with less exploration. A narrative review of mostly sub-clinical, unreplicated studies with inconsistent tasks and measures. |

| [LIT-1490](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1490.md) v2 | Impaired action-safety learning and excessive relief during avoidance in patients with anxiety disorders | De Kleine, Hutschemaekers, Hendriks, Kampman, Papalini, Van Minnen & Vervliet (2023). In a computer-based avoidance task, 47 healthy controls were compared with 33 patients with OCD, 40 with panic disorder with agoraphobia and 66 with PTSD, before exposure treatment. OCD and PTSD patients avoided more during the safety cue and kept a higher expectancy of the aversive picture after the safety cue and after effective avoidance; PDA and PTSD patients reported more relief. The groups did not differ in avoiding the danger cues. The authors propose that low confidence in the safety that avoidance brings makes omissions surprising, and the extra relief reinforces avoidance. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1123](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1123.md)) from the CC BY version of record; worth reading as, by its own count, the third experimental study of avoidance learning in anxiety patients, and the first to track what they learn from avoiding as well as how often they avoid. Against 47 controls, OCD and PTSD patients avoided a safety cue more and, after effective avoidance, still expected the aversive picture more; PDA and PTSD patients reported more relief at omissions; nobody differed on the danger cues. Cross-sectional, with no cost to avoiding; relief was already higher before avoidance was possible, and patients rated the pictures as more aversive. That the excess relief reinforces avoidance is the authors' interpretation, not a finding. |
| [LIT-1491](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1491.md) v2 | The standalone effect of safety behavior manipulations: A systematic review and meta-analysis | Goodson, Patel, Zech, Sala & Cougle (2026). Of 26 studies of standalone safety-behaviour manipulations outside exposure (2,048 participants, mean age 24.9), 19 were meta-analysed. Relative to control, reducing safety behaviours reduced them (d = 0.52, 95% CI 0.36–0.68, after one outlier was removed) and reduced symptoms (d = 0.43, 95% CI 0.27–0.59; 0.31 after trim-and-fill, Egger p = .012); increasing them, in five non-clinical experiments, raised safety behaviours (d = 2.96) and symptoms (d = 0.65). Only study type (for the effect on safety behaviours) and the size of the safety-behaviour change (for symptoms) moderated the effects. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1128](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1128.md)) from the NIH author manuscript in PubMed Central, not the closed version of record; worth reading as the first meta-analysis of safety-behaviour manipulations made outside exposure. Reducing them lowered symptoms against control (d = 0.43, about 0.31 after trim-and-fill, with significant Egger asymmetry), instructed increases raised symptoms (d = 0.65, five studies), and the size of the safety-behaviour change moderated the symptom effect. The literature is small, mostly appearance and social anxiety in young, largely non-clinical samples, and largely from the senior author's group. It says nothing about how safety behaviours act. |

| [LIT-1496](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1496.md) v2 | Anxiety, Avoidance, and Sequential Evaluation | Zorowitz, Momennejad & Daw (2020; preprint 2019). A decision-theoretic analysis and reinforcement-learning simulations of maladaptive avoidance, with no data fitted. In sequential evaluation the chance to avoid danger later should make it less threatening now; a pessimistic false belief that one's own later avoidance will fail, with the danger represented correctly, propagates fear and avoidance to situations far before the threat. This one bias reproduces qualitatively exaggerated threat appraisal, fear generalization, persistent avoidance and laboratory findings on approach–avoid conflict and loss avoidance, and predicts a reduced free-choice premium in anxiety. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1136](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1136.md)) from the CC BY version of record; worth reading for the derivation that avoidance far from a threat needs no overestimate of the threat, only an expectation that one will fail to avoid it later, which spreads threat value backward across a decision process. Simulations only, matched qualitatively to published findings (earlier cash-out, behavioural inhibition, aversive pruning); the predicted loss of the free-choice premium is untested, and the persistence of avoidance after the misbelief is corrected is argued, not simulated. |
| [LIT-1498](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1498.md) v2 | Behavior as information: “If I avoid, then there must be a danger” | Gangemi, Mancini & van den Hout (2012). Anxious participants (31 with obsessive-compulsive disorder, 22 with panic, 17 with social phobia) and 31 controls rated danger in scripts that varied objective danger and the presence of a safety behaviour. Anxious participants inferred danger from the safety behaviour as well as from objective information, while controls were influenced mainly by objective danger; the effect was disorder-specific for social phobia and OCD. Taking one's own safety behaviour as evidence of danger may maintain anxiety. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-24 from the owner's exchange of 2026-10-23/24, shared at https://chatgpt.com/share/6adc1ece-bb28-83e9-a8f6-cadf0f8b7113, where it is cited at turn U15; a reading was attempted on 2026-10-24 and failed on availability: no lawful full text was found. | [LIT-1500](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1500.md) v2 | Maximizing exposure therapy: An inhibitory learning approach | Craske, Treanor, Conway, Zbozinek & Vervliet (2014). A clinical translation of the inhibitory-learning model of extinction: the original threat association survives extinction, beside a competing inhibitory one, so fear can return; fear reduction during exposure does not predict outcome; and exposure should be designed to violate stated expectancies, not to reduce fear in session. Strategies: expectancy violation, deepened extinction, occasional reinforced extinction, removal of safety signals, variability, retrieval cues, multiple contexts and reconsolidation, with affect labeling as a further regulation strategy. Cognitive restructuring before exposure is held to blunt learning. Five illustrative cases; no new data. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1137](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1137.md)) from the NIH author manuscript in PubMed Central, the accepted unedited version, not the closed version of record; worth reading as the standard clinical statement of the inhibitory-learning account of exposure: extinction adds a competing inhibitory association and leaves the original intact, fear reduction during exposure does not predict outcome, and exposure should be built to violate expectancies. It reports no data. Its strategies are cited to evidence of uneven strength, which the authors flag, and it reports the evidence against removing safety behaviours as well as for it. |
| [LIT-1685](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1685.md) | Trauma, prejudice, large-group identity and psychoanalysis | A memorial lecture, not a study. Volkan defines a large group as thousands or millions of people who mostly never meet but share sentiments, and pictures large-group identity as a tent's canvas worn over each member's individual identity, with the leader as its pole. Membership in ethnic, national and religious groups begins in childhood, through identification with parents' investment in the group and the images and "ego tasks" they deposit in the child; after adolescence a core large-group identity cannot be changed. From unofficial dialogues between conflicting groups (1980s to early 2000s), he reports that the central psychological factor in large-group conflict is the need to protect large-group identity, and that a participant who felt that identity threatened would speak with emotion of an injury suffered by ancestors centuries before. The shared image of such an event, "real, fantasized or even mythologized", undergoes a change of function as it passes down the generations and becomes an identity marker: a chosen trauma. Chosen traumas feed entitlement ideologies and, in a "time collapse", make the old event feel recent, as Milošević did with Kosovo 1389, with dehumanization and purification following. Recent traumas, the Holocaust among them, are not chosen traumas but undigested ones, bound up with large-group mourning. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1250](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1250.md)), in place of [LIT-1727](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1727.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as Volkan's late, short restatement of chosen trauma, its trigger in threatened identity and its distinction from the mourning of recent trauma, read in place of his 2001 paper; the evidence is his own clinical and diplomatic observation, without method or measure. |

The samples are small, and the paper is widely cited and widely criticized. | Unfetched — filed 2026-10-29, not read; set Unfetched the same day under [ADR-053](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-053.md): the publisher's copy is free to read at biologicalpsychiatryjournal.com (doi:10.1016/j.biopsych.2015.08.005), listed by Unpaywall as bronze; it is not in PMC and has no author manuscript. Read in its place, and not a substitute for reading it: Youssef et al. 2018 (LIT-1725). |
| [LIT-1694](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1694.md) | "Surviving Early Childhood Trauma: Effects of the Holocaust on Survivors' Psychological and Physiological Well-Being" | A Leiden thesis of four empirical papers on one Israeli sample drawn from the population registry: female child survivors who lost both parents in the Holocaust, matched women who emigrated from Europe to Palestine with their parents before it, and the daughters of both. More than 60 years on, survivors reported more dissociation, less life satisfaction, more cognitive impairment and more stress from recent life events. They had higher diurnal cortisol and an anomalous response to a laboratory stressor, and in an exploratory analysis this held only for ADRA2B wildtype carriers. Their daughters did not differ from comparison daughters on any psychological, cognitive, health or cortisol measure. The one intergenerational signal: daughters of more dissociative survivors had lower diurnal cortisol (n = 17 against 10). The introduction and discussions restate the authors' two meta-analyses, which found no second- or third-generation traumatization in non-clinical, well-designed samples. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1291](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1291.md)), in place of [LIT-1718](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1718.md) and [LIT-1770](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1770.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as the record's only account, at second hand and by their own authors' student, of the 2003 and 2008 meta-analyses ([LIT-1718](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1718.md), [LIT-1770](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1770.md), both Unavailable), and as a primary two-generation study whose matched design holds national identity constant and finds no family transmission. |

| [LIT-1725](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1725.md) | The Effects of Trauma, with or without PTSD, on the Transgenerational DNA Methylation Alterations in Human Offsprings | Youssef et al. (2018). A short narrative review of human studies of parental trauma and offspring DNA methylation, PubMed to March 2018. It finds two studies of parents and children: Rwandan mothers pregnant during the genocide (25 exposed, 25 abroad), with higher NR3C1 methylation and lower cortisol in mothers and children; and Holocaust survivors (32) and offspring (22) against 8 controls and their 9 offspring, with higher FKBP5 intron 7 methylation in survivors and lower in their offspring. Three more concern stress in pregnancy (Congo, intimate partner violence) and NR3C1 methylation in newborns and adolescents. The authors call the evidence accumulating but preliminary: small samples, cross-sectional designs, unmeasured confounds, possible publication bias. They use "transgenerational" for any parent-to-child effect, in utero exposure included. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1310](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1310.md)), in place of [LIT-1692](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1692.md), which could not be fetched here; worth reading as a brief, sympathetic account of the Holocaust FKBP5 study and the few human studies beside it, by authors not on that study (though Rutten has published with its second author, Daskalakis; ref. 13). |

| [LIT-1736](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1736.md) | Multigenerational legacies of trauma: Modeling the what and how of transmission | A web survey of 422 adult children of Holocaust survivors, a convenience sample recruited through survivor and Jewish organizations, tests Danieli's 1998 framework, Trauma and the Continuity of Self, as a path model. The children rated their parents' posttrauma styles (victim, numb, fighter), their own "reparative adaptational impacts" and their family's history. Parents' Holocaust experiences, internment above all, were linked to the children's impacts only indirectly, through the parents' victim style, and those indirect effects were small (.05 to .06). Post-war family milieu mattered more than wartime history. Settling in Israel rather than North America, surviving grandparents, larger surviving families and religious continuity went with milder impacts. Broken generational linkages (rarely thinking of one's murdered grandparents as one's own, and remembering the family's history "only in bits and pieces") had the largest total effect, and the only direct one. There was no comparison group and every measure came from the child. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1307](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1307.md)), in place of [LIT-1701](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1701.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as the clinical tradition's own quantitative test of the parenting route, and for its finding that descendants who count their murdered grandparents as their own fare better, not worse; read in place of the 1998 handbook ([LIT-1701](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1701.md)). |

| [LIT-1774](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1774.md) | Inter- and transgenerational inheritance of behavioral phenotypes | Jawaid & Mansuy (2019). A short review from Mansuy's laboratory, the proponents' side. Rodent studies show that parental trauma, stress, drugs and in-utero insults pass behavioural phenotypes to offspring, in some models to the third or fourth generation, and that parental environmental enrichment passes benefits, and can prevent the transmission of trauma's effects. Germline dependence is shown by IVF and by injecting sperm RNA, which reproduces the phenotypes; non-coding RNAs are the best candidate carriers. Human studies of genocide survivors' descendants are offered as similar, and the review itself tables them as intergenerational. How a stimulus reaches the germline, and how effects pass beyond the first generation, are unknown. Germline reprogramming and the sceptics' objections are not discussed. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1296](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1296.md)), in place of [LIT-1738](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1738.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as the proponents' short statement of the rodent case for germline transmission of behaviour, read in place of Bohacek and Mansuy 2015 ([LIT-1738](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1738.md)), and for what it does not answer. |
